query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the coupled tribo‐corrosion response is governed by the balance between the mechanical removal of a self‐forming passive oxide film and its ability to reform. When mechanical wear exceeds the oxide film regeneration rate, the barrier is compromised and exposes fresh metal to corrosive attack, leading to a synergistic increase in overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy processed to develop a homogeneous microstructure and an in-situ, self-passivating oxide layer (e.g., rich in Cr, Al, or similar alloying elements) achieved via a controlled heat treatment and atmospheric exposure.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled tribo‐corrosion study by using a reciprocating tribometer integrated with an electrochemical cell. Run tests at varying mechanical contact loads (or sliding speeds) to modulate the wear intensity while keeping the chemical (corrosive electrolyte) conditions constant. Compare the results with static corrosion and wear-only tests to isolate the effect of the oxide film removal.
generation.conditions: Tests are carried out at ambient temperature in a 3.5% NaCl solution (or similar chloride electrolyte) at neutral pH. The tribometer applies controlled normal loads and constant sliding speeds, with tests lasting for durations long enough to allow steady-state passive film reformation in static conditions. Baseline experiments include static immersion tests with no mechanical loading and wear tests in an inert (non-corrosive) environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and regeneration rate of the passive oxide film that forms on the high-entropy alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: Under tribological loading in a corrosive medium, mechanical wear disrupts the passivating oxide film faster than it can self-heal. This removal leads to unprotected regions that suffer accelerated corrosion. In comparison, static conditions allow the film to remain intact or reform, limiting degradation. Therefore, when wear exceeds a critical threshold, the coupling between mechanical abrasion and corrosion synergistically increases the degradation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to higher mechanical wear will exhibit significantly greater total degradation compared to matched static corrosion and wear-only baselines, with a concomitant increase in corrosion rates (e.g., higher current densities in polarization tests) and increased wear volume. This prediction should hold for alloys with a robust, self-healing passive film and may fail in alloys where the passive film is inherently unstable or at temperatures where film kinetics are altered.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples that experience either static corrosion (allowing complete passive film development) or minimal wear (where the protective oxide remains largely intact).
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to be valid in environments where a self-healing passive oxide is readily formed (e.g., moderate temperatures, neutral pH). It may not hold in conditions where the alloy’s passivation is poor (due to composition or extreme environmental factors) or when the mechanical loading is too low to affect the film.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative wear-load threshold at which the passive film fails to regenerate quickly enough is uncertain and will require precise experimental calibration. Moreover, interactions between microstructural heterogeneities and local corrosion behavior add additional layers of complexity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical high-entropy alloy samples with the same initial passive film. Test them under two distinct regimes using a tribometer integrated with electrochemical testing: one with a low, sub-threshold contact load where the film is expected to remain largely intact, and one with a high load presumed sufficient to mechanically remove the film. Simultaneously, run a static corrosion test as a control. Monitor the evolution of the passive film integrity in real time using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and post-test surface analysis (e.g., SEM, XPS) to correlate film presence with corrosion behavior.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization curves to assess corrosion rate
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for film integrity
Surface morphology and compositional mapping (SEM, XPS) post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-load (high wear) samples do not show a significant increase in corrosion rates or overall degradation compared to the low-load and static corrosion controls—or if the passive film appears unaffected by increased mechanical loading—then the hypothesis that wear-induced removal of the passive film is the governing mechanism in tribo-corrosion would be falsified.
